name: Apache Flink
summary: A distributed data-processing runtime that executes stateful and timely stream dataflows through JobManagers, TaskManagers, operator tasks, keyed state, and checkpoint-based recovery.

features.name: JobManager and TaskManager runtime
features.description: Flink separates coordination and execution between JobManagers and TaskManagers. JobManagers coordinate scheduling, checkpoints, and recovery, while TaskManagers execute tasks and exchange buffered data streams; task slots are the basic scheduling unit.
benefits: Separates global coordination from worker execution
Supports multiple resource providers and cluster deployment modes
Makes task parallelism and resource allocation explicit
costs: Coordination and worker failure require distributed recovery
Task slots reserve managed memory but do not provide full CPU isolation
Deployment mode changes cluster lifecycle and resource-sharing behavior

features.name: Operator chaining and parallel subtasks
features.description: Flink chains compatible operator subtasks into tasks. Each task executes in one thread, while parallel subtasks run across TaskManagers and share task-slot resources according to the job's parallelism and slot-sharing configuration.
benefits: Reduces handoff and buffering overhead between chained operators
Expresses dataflow parallelism as independently scheduled subtasks
Improves resource utilization through same-job slot sharing
costs: Chaining can make task boundaries less visible during diagnosis
Shared slots couple memory and JVM failure domains
Parallelism and partitioning choices affect throughput and state movement

features.name: Keyed state and checkpoint recovery
features.description: Flink partitions keyed state together with keyed streams and uses distributed checkpoints to capture source positions and operator state. Recovery restores the latest completed checkpoint and replays input from the recorded positions.
benefits: Keeps state access local to the current event key
Supports rescaling by redistributing state through key groups
Provides a documented path to consistent recovery and exactly-once processing semantics
costs: Checkpoint storage and coordination add runtime overhead
Strong guarantees depend on rewindable sources and compatible sinks
Large state increases checkpoint, recovery, and rescaling cost

features.name: Event-time watermarks and windows
features.description: Flink distinguishes processing time from event time. Watermarks advance an operator's event-time clock and permit windows to process out-of-order data, while multi-input operators advance according to the minimum input watermark.
benefits: Makes event timestamps rather than machine clocks drive window semantics
Provides a protocol for bounded waiting on out-of-order events
Allows time- and data-driven windows over unbounded streams
costs: Late events and finite watermark delays limit determinism
Waiting for event-time progress adds latency
Watermark alignment across inputs can hold back downstream progress

mathematical_views.question: Which state and input positions must be restored to reproduce a consistent distributed stream computation after failure?
assumptions: Operators and sources expose serializable state and positions
Checkpoint barriers define a consistent cut through the dataflow
Sources can rewind to the recorded positions and side effects are modeled separately

mathematical_views.question: How does event-time progress propagate through parallel and multi-input operators?
assumptions: Each input carries an event-time watermark
A multi-input operator's progress is bounded by the minimum input watermark
Late data and allowed lateness are explicit parts of the model

benefits: Efficient parallel execution with configurable sharing
costs: Resource and debugging boundaries become configuration-sensitive
State snapshots consume storage, I/O, and recovery time

benefits: Time semantics remain tied to event data
costs: Out-of-order handling introduces latency and lateness policy
